November 16, 1987
Adjournment Debate
RAILWAYS-DELAY IN GRAIN DELIVERIES TO THUNDER BAY-NEED FOR MORE HOPPER CARS/DOM1NION MARINE ASSOCIATION'S REQUEST FOR ACTION

Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to take a few moments this evening to consider further questions which I directed to the Government on November 2. I will quote from my question at that time to make it quite clear what we are dealing with. Speaking to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) I said:
He is undoubtedly aware that for more than a month the railways have failed to deliver enough grain to the Port of Thunder Bay to meet commitments there. Ships have been lying idle in the harbour and workers on lay-off when they would like to be at work moving grain into the ships.
I then asked:
When does the Government intend to recognize the need for more hopper cars on the Prairies in order to move grain? In particular, when does it plan to ensure that the CNR is up to the challenge it faces in keeping our grain moving?
Those are the questions, Madam Speaker, which become more and more important. The focus here is specifically on the situation in Thunder Bay but I fear the problem will become worse as the grain transportation system we operate in western Canada faces increasing demands on it. I want to be very sure that we do not have to discriminate in any direction in dealing with this particular challenge.
We want to be sure that the railways have the rolling stock to get the product there when it needs to flow to market. We want to be sure that no markets are lost. We want to be sure that farmers have the satisfaction of knowing that their produce is moving. We do not want to see the wastage of ships lying idle in harbours. Certainly in Thunder Bay we would like to see as many grain handlers as possible working in the elevators.
I am concerned, as a Member of Parliament from Thunder Bay, about this issue. We must solve it in a way which will recognize the needs of people on the Prairies, the concerns of the producers, the desire of grain farmers to get their produce to market. We must do that in a way which will save us from having to discriminate against the Seaway in favour of the West Coast or, conceivably, for us in Thunder Bay to be arguing for a slow-down on the West Coast, which has a year round operation, in order that we can get it in before the frost comes. I do not want to be forced to make that kind of argument.
I recognize, of course, that we are in a situation, at least briefly, of large sales. How could I be anything but very happy about that on behalf of the farmers and everyone involved in transporting the product? I would like to think that the present situation is likely to continue in the future and that we are going beyond the slow times which we have known in the last couple of years. Let this be the new reality. Assuming that it will be, we face a very real challenge.
In Thunder Bay this fall the Wheat Board was calling for movement which would require as much as 6,000 cars a week.
In fact, by the end of October we really needed 7,000 cars weekly at the elevator in Thunder Bay in order to meet the demand. We did not get those. We rarely topped 4,000 cars per week during September and October. As a result, the people of Thunder Bay began to see ships lying idle in the harbour again.
From one perspective there was a happy feature to that. We had been told at the beginning of July that Thunder Bay was going to be residual in the grain movement system. We began to worry. A lot of concern was expressed in Thunder Bay during July that all the emphasis was on the West Coast. We were concerned about where that would leave the Seaway. It was, therefore, nice to know that there was so much demand from the Atlantic markets through the Seaway that we could not meet it.
However, we do not want to be content with that. We want to be sure that we are up to the demand. When the CNR closed Churchill it released 3,000 cars and, as the media reported, it may be capable of bringing us 1,500 a week in Thunder Bay. If we had hit 4,200-and I pick that number because it is over 4,000, although I am not sure we would actually hit 4,200 in one of those weeks-and if we add 1,500 rather smaller boxcars to it, we are still at only 5,700 or so. If the need by the beginning of November was for 7,000 cars weekly, the railways were clearly not up to it. CP Rail apparently did better at this particular challenge by turning to U.S. railways to lease the hopper cars or whatever rolling stock was required. It managed to keep up. CNR clearly did not.
The Minister spoke of records, but I am not sure if those records extend back over all the years of terrific movement. However, we are doing very well on a daily or weekly basis. Let us be ready for that and not have to depend on American railways being able to release rolling stock to us.
Let us also recognize that old boxcars are being taken out of service. There is clearly a need for the Government to recognize this not only as a challenge but as an opportunity. Rolling stock could be produced in factories in this country. It is a marvellous opportunity to put the Trenton Works to use. I am not arguing for CanCar in Thunder Bay because it is busy with subway cars and so on. Let us provide the work in a place in Atlantic Canada where the Government also wants to see more people employed. People on the Prairies and the Mari-times can be satisfied at the same time. That is all Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, through the middle of September, sales projections for October/November at Thunder Bay stood at 2.2 million tonnes, and the railways had planned accordingly.
Also, my friend is aware of the very sophisticated process that generally works very well for predicting the cars, allocating them and moving grain to the ports. That system works very well as a result of several hundred people working very
November 16, 1987

closely together and with a high level of goodwill and cooperation.
As my colleague, the Hon. Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer), stated earlier today, Canadian exports are up some 18 per cent over last year's and last year in itself was a record year. I suppose these are the problems we would like to have. If we could solve the price problem we could have the country hitting on all cylinders as compared to now when we are experiencing some problems in the West. Indeed, I believe that Canada's market share is up to 24 per cent from 17 per cent in spite of the enormous battle between the EEC and the United States. That is good news for Canada, subject to price.
CP has some 3,000 leased cars and is bringing its total fleet to approximately 14,000 cars, approximately 7,000 of which are in service to Thunder Bay. CN's total grain fleet is 14,700 cars with the 3,000 boxcars from Churchill, about 6,000 in service now in Thunder Bay. A very tight North American lease market for hopper cars has limited attempts to add further to the fleets.
One must consider whether the railways should be staffing for these peaks that were unpredictable. Of course, we should be making changes for the future and I would be interested to hear my friend's view as to where that money should be obtained, whether in the public domain or by the railways. How does one then justify the carrying costs of the cars if shipments should decline? These are problems that are being addressed by the system.
The Grain Transportation Agency is currently undertaking an extensive review of the system car capacity to determine current and future car needs. At present, a full review is being undertaken by the Minister through the Grain Transportation Agency and he is monitoring the situation carefully.
I am sure this can be resolved. I believe some 6,200 cars were unloaded last week and 6,500 are expected this week. Hopefully that will help to alleviate the problem.
AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-ORANT MADE TO EDMONTON AMUSEMENT PARK PROJECT/ORDER IN COUNCIL QUERY

Madam Speaker, on November 3, I asked the Government about the $4.5 million contribution which had been made to Fantasyland in the West Edmonton Mall. I asked the question because 1 had studied the legal background of the Government's authority to make the grant and I had read the Auditor General's Report. I came to the conclusion that as far as I was concerned there was no legal basis for making that grant.
This morning I received a letter from someone who lives in Edmonton accusing me of being anti-west and arguing that 1 had no business attacking something that was so important to Edmonton and so valuable to the people there. It was a basis for tourism and so on. What happened today is that I am already beginning to harvest the poisonous crops the Prime
Adjournment Debate
Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) sowed about this issue when he accused people who criticized that grant of being antiwestern.
My enthusiasm about western Canada I think is pretty well known. I have been to the West Edmonton Mall, I like it, and I am appalled that I have to write a letter to those people defending my belief that western Canada should have its aspirations supported by the Government. This is what I was talking about. It is just this simple. The Auditor General of Canada, whom I do not think even the Prime Minister accuses of being anti-western, analysed the contribution and found it was made in violation of the regulations.
The Industrial and Regional Development Act authorizes the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) to make a grant or contribution to a commercial operation in respect of a project carried out or to be carried out for a purpose set out in any of paragraphs 4(1 )(a) to (d) of the Act. I am reading from an anti-western tract. As per Section 2 of the Act, a commercial operation is a commercial operation as defined by the regulations. To qualify, if it is a service industry, it has to be designated by order of the Minister pursuant to subsection 7(2) of the Act. Well, there is no order designated pursuant to subsection 7(2) of the Act.
As a member of the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, I have easy access to the list of all the orders and all the publications and it does not appear. What that means, in my examination of the law, is that this contribution cannot stand and, as the Act says, when a contribution is made in violation of the Act without authorization under the Act, it has to be treated as a loan. The recipient has to give it back. That was the question I asked.
What is appalling is that when a Member of Parliament stands up to ask a question like this based on what the Auditor General says about the law, and on the fact that the Province of Alberta felt that this project did not need any money from the Government-and the Province of Alberta is not antiwestern-and the fact that the former Government refused it because it did not think it came within the terms of the Act, it is said that that member is anti-western. The officials of the Government told the Minister that he did not have the authority under the regulations to make that grant. The Minister failed to pass the order, to have it published in the Canada Gazette, which could have validated it.
There was another illustration over the weekend of a Prime Minister and a Government which is determined to have their way, dividing this country by going out west and telling westerners that the reason Ontario is against free trade is because it does not want to see the west prosper.
That type of approach is so damaging to our country that I think again and again Members of the House have to stand up and criticize the Government for doing this. If it cannot defend its policies on the basis of national reconciliation, which is the platform the Government ran on and promised to deliver, if it cannot find ways of strengthening national unity, it seems the

November 16, 1987
Adjournment Debate
only way it can sell its act is on the basis of pitting one part of Canada against the other when there is no foundation for doing so.
This is a country made up of diverse regions. Very often issues arise. When we have an extra dollar in the till of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to spend, it has to be decided what region is going to get it, where will the CF-18s be built. It is tough enough when something like that comes along, but to go around inventing them gratuitously to try to get westerners feeling that the Hon. Member for York Centre and the people of Ontario are against them realizing their aspirations just because we want to be the only ones in Ontario who are well off is a form of regional racism. To see a Government go ahead and make arguments like that is so unworthy that one can only hope that members of that caucus at their regular meeting on Wednesday will read the riot act to the Prime Minister and ask him to get his act together and stop making false accusations that amount to a form of regional racism.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the distinguished Member's argument is sophisticated. He is trying to do by one means that which he could not do by another. That is to say, justify the grounds for his question to the Government of the other day. The former Minister has suggested that he has researched the law. The fact of the matter is that he has not researched the case at all. I say that with some deference to the hon. gentleman.
The response I wish to give to the Hon. Member is precisely that which I gave in the late show on November 2. If the hon. gentleman is particularly interested he can refer to page 10658 of Hansard. I will quote from the position put forward by DRIE. Let me just say as a preface that the application in 1983, when it was received, was clearly eligible as a tourism operation under the regulations that were in effect at that time and continued to be eligible for consideration after the November, 1984 amendments, since no rejection was ever communicated to the applicant. Accordingly, no order in council was required. The hon. gentleman is a learned scholar of the law. I suggest he either overlooked that or found it convenient not to complete it.
The position of DRIE at the time, a position which continues to the best of my knowledge, is as follows, and I quote from Hansard:
-the application for assistance for this project was received on December 7, 1983 and while tourism was dropped from IRDP on November 9, 1984 the application was protected under the grandfather provisions. It is clear from file documentation that the necessary permits, construction contracts and actual construction on this project was/were not entered into prior to December 7, 1983 and therefore the project was not prior committed within the terms of Section 29(1) of the pre-November 9, 1984 regulations to the IRDP. DRIE's position remains that the project continued to be eligible for assistance consideration under IRDP, notwithstanding the fact that the construction was well advanced in August, 1985 when the DRIE Minister made the actual
decision to assist... The IRDP contribution facilitated the company in arranging the additional financing and consequently ensured that the project was completed within the originally proposed scope and timing. If DRIE had not offered the assistance at that time, it is highly probable that construction would have been delayed and the significant contributions that have accrued to Canada's economy over the past two years from this tourism facility would have been substantially lessened.
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-VISITS BY NUCLEAR POWERED VESSELS TO ESQUIMALT/RESULTS OF GOVERNMENT INQUIRY

Mr. Speaker, on November 5, I asked the Government for its response to a study done by Professor Jackson Davis of the University of California at Santa Cruz on the possible effects of a nuclear accident involving a nuclear-powered and/or a nuclear-armed submarine happening to visit Esquimalt, British Columbia. The possible effects of that as outlined by Professor Davis are absolutely horrendous.
He predicts two scenarios. The first deals with the incineration of a single nuclear warhead on a shipboard fire. The second deals with a hypothetical nuclear reactor accident. I would like to read about the possibility of an accident involving a nuclear warhead. The report states:
Such an accident would produce a radioactive cloud containing plutonium-239, which would be carried toward the northeast, directly over Esquimalt/Victoria, by the most probable prevailing winds. The plutonium concentration in the cloud would exceed U.S. federal (NRC) limits for air contamination (10 CFR 20) by up to ten thousand times. Ground contamination from fallout would exceed U.S. federal (NRC) limits for unrestricted public use by up to one million times. Radiation exposure from inhalation of the plutonium would exceed U.S. federal limits for "routine" releases by up to one hundred thousand times.
Prompt fatalities have not been considered here; instead casualties calculated here would take the form of latent cancers fatalities and genetic defects. Latent cancer fatalities incurred during the accident would range from 15 to 3,413 depending on thermal lofting, atmospheric stability and the radiation risk factor used, with an equal number of additional fatalities from severe genetic defects. The greatest contamination would occur nearest the accident site, although both air and ground contamination would remain well above the NRC limits up to 50 km from the accident site and beyond . . . Under unfavourable meteorological conditions the effects of such an accident could be experienced as far away as Vancouver.
Jackson Davis points out the excessive costs that would be involved in any attempt to clean up after an accident of this type. He also points out that we are completely lacking in any type of public program to deal with that type of emergency.
Last week in Victoria some 2,000 school children were involved in an emergency preparation involving the possibility of an earthquake. There has not been a major earthquake in Victoria of the type that they are considering within the recorded historical period, but it is a possibility and it had to be considered with children being involved.
For any accident involving nuclear vessels in Canadian ports, the emergency procedures are not made public so that the public does not know what is expected of them or what is to be done. Any worth-while emergency procedure has to be made public.
November 16, 1987

In view of the findings of Professor Davis' study, I raised three recommendations. The first was that the Government should discard its plans to purchase nuclear submarines for Canada. This is not only an expensive boondoggling exercise that will not contribute to Canadian security, but it also poses a real danger and threat to Canadian ports. Second, we should cease to honour the United States refusal to confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on board vessels visiting Canadian ports. Third, we should review the entire policy of allowing nuclear powered vessels to visit Canadian harbours. The visit of foreign warships to the harbours of another country is an old established practice, and no doubt it had some value as a gesture of friendship in earlier times.
But today when we are talking about nuclear vessels that are powered with nuclear reactors, it is the same as siting a nuclear reactor within a densely populated urban area. Admittedly, the probability of an accident is low, but there has been Three Mile Island, and there have been accidents aboard nuclear powered submarines in the past.
Countries such as New Zealand and Iceland have taken a stand against allowing nuclear armed vessels to visit their harbours. Australia prohibits nuclear powered vessels from visiting the large Port of Sydney. There are only three ports in Canada which allow nuclear powered submarines to visit, namely, Esquimalt, Nanoose, and Halifax, which is right next to the riding of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary.
If the Government decided that it was to allow these visits to continue, it should very seriously consider the recommendations of Doctor Jackson Davis when he said:
Evacuation plans should be established, co-ordinated and rehearsed periodically . . . Decontamination plans in the event of an accident should likewise be formulated-The data needed to ascertain empirically the probability of nuclear accidents should be obtained from the U.S. military so that the risk to the Canadian public can be estimated as closely as possible ... Detailed liability and indemnity regimes in the event of an accident should be negotiated in advance . . . Existing emergency response institutions, procedures and documents should be evaluated in light of accident analyses such as the present one.
In response to an early concern about this, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said that Canada had done its own study and assured me that Canadians were protected. I would ask that the Government release the study to Canadians so that they can determine for themselves how well they are protected.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all let me point out to the Hon. Member that nuclear propulsion is not new technology. Second, there has been no nuclear accident in the 34-year history of the allied nuclear naval program. Nuclear powered warships have steamed over 100 million kilometres and have accumulated over 3,200 reactor-years of
Adjournment Debate
operating experience. In that connection, I do not think that these ships or vessels or submarines carry anywhere near the size of the nuclear plant facility as was suggested by the Hon. Member.
The study recently released by Greenpeace on port safety is less a description of reality than a hypothetical model and, as such, can be manipulated to demonstrate any point that a speaker or author might want to make. Given the preconditions, assumptions, and pure guesses of what might happen, or what might influence conditions if an accident occurred, most of the resulting conclusions are necessarily speculative.
The model presented in the Greenpeace study does not support the need for an inquiry. What it does support is the need to make proper provision for safety co-ordination. Although the model suggests that, in a worst case scenario, thousands of Canadians could be put at risk, even the study recognizes the extremely low probability of such an accident. Finally, it should be borne in mind that accidents which have occurred to nuclear propelled and armed submarines have not resulted in radioactive pollutants being released into the environment.
Let me also assure you, Madam Speaker, that the Canadian Government is committed to keeping the Canadian public well informed on all safety related aspects of such naval visits and its own program to acquire nuclear propelled submarines. As a start in this process, general information briefing sessions have been initiated by DND. Two, one in Ottawa and the other in Esquimalt, have already taken place.
Furthermore, these media and background briefings will continue to take place until the final decision on the country of origin of the submarine is made. After that time the briefings and information dissemination will concentrate on explaining safety elements peculiar to the selected type. It should be noted that both of the submarines now being evaluated have impressive safety records and, security questions aside, a considerable amount of information supporting the safety of nuclear propelled submarines is already in the public domain.
The Government does not underestimate the need for detailed consideration of all safety aspects of nuclear propelled submarines and the elaboration of the highest standards for their safe operation. The Government is already actively engaged in an in-depth evaluation and planning process that is being carried out by specialized units at DND, ACEL, and AECB. The Hon. Member will be made aware of these detailed plans as they proceed.
